claims.source: Secondary summaries (BetterUp, ModelThinkers, thinkinsights.net) found by search on 13 November 2026; the book itself was not checked.

claims.claim: Issue trees with a hypothesis and a test per branch, ranked by size and speed, are common consulting practice.
claims.source: General practice, not a quotation from one source.

concept_html:
Requests arrive vague: "Why is attrition up?" If you start pulling data at once, you answer whatever the first chart suggests. An issue tree gives you a plan first.

The tree. Write the question at the top. Split it into two to five sub-questions, then split each again until every leaf is a question one piece of analysis answers. "Why is voluntary attrition up?" splits into "Which people are leaving?" and "Why are they leaving?". "Which people?" splits by grade, by function or by tenure.

The MECE test. At each split, check two things:

  • Mutually exclusive: no item sits in two branches. "Graduates" and "London staff" overlap, so a London graduate is counted twice.
  • Collectively exhaustive: the branches cover everything. "Engineering" and "Sales" miss Finance and HR.

Splits that follow a definition pass the test by design: leavers are voluntary or involuntary, and every employee has one grade.

Hypotheses. For each branch, write the answer you expect and the analysis that would prove or disprove it. "Leavers cluster in their first year, because onboarding changed in March. Test: attrition by tenure band, before and after March."

Prune. Drop branches whose answer would not change the decision. Rank the rest by likely size and by how quickly you can test them.

The MECE idea comes from Barbara Minto's work at McKinsey, set out in The Pyramid Principle (Minto, editions from 1987).

lines: Why is voluntary attrition up this year?
Who is leaving?
By tenure band: under 1 year, 1 to 3 years, over 3 years
Hypothesis: first-year leavers rose after onboarding changed in March
Test: attrition by tenure band, before and after March
By location: one row per site
Hypothesis: one site drives the rise
Test: leavers per site against headcount per site
Why are they leaving?
Pay, manager, career, workload, other
Hypothesis: career reasons rose most
Test: exit reasons, coded on one list, this year against last

example.takeaway_html: Turn a vague question into a tree of sub-questions. Make each split mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, give each branch a hypothesis and a test, and drop branches that would not change the decision.

exercises.primer:
Sets support three operators you need here:

```python
a = {"x", "y"}
b = {"y", "z"}
a & b   # {"y"}, in both
a | b   # {"x", "y", "z"}, in either
a - b   # {"x"}, in a but not in b
```

`set()` makes an empty set, and `sorted(some_set)` returns its items as a sorted list.

exercises.prompt_html:
Write mece_check(population: set[str], branches: dict[str, set[str]]) -> dict[str, list[str]]. population holds the IDs of every item, such as every leaver. branches maps each branch name to the IDs it covers.

Return a dict with three keys, each holding a sorted list of IDs:

  • "overlap": IDs in more than one branch;
  • "gap": IDs in the population but in no branch;
  • "outside": IDs in a branch but not in the population.

A MECE split returns three empty lists.
exercises.solution:
def mece_check(population: set[str], branches: dict[str, set[str]]) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    """Check that branches split a population with no overlap and no gaps.

    Args:
        population: Every item ID the question covers.
        branches: Branch name to the item IDs it covers.

    Returns:
        Sorted IDs under "overlap" (in two or more branches), "gap" (in no branch)
        and "outside" (in a branch but not the population).
    """
    seen: set[str] = set()
    repeated: set[str] = set()
    for members in branches.values():
        repeated |= seen & members
        seen |= members
    return {
        "overlap": sorted(repeated),
        "gap": sorted(population - seen),
        "outside": sorted(seen - population),
    }

title: Break a vague question into an issue tree
why_html: An analyst asked "why is attrition up?" spent two weeks on exit survey themes. The rise came from one site that closed, which a split by location would have shown on the first day. An issue tree with a location branch, tested first because it was quick, would have saved the two weeks.
